statements.quote: To answer this research question, we used data collected for a previous study (under review) focusing on human-AI brainstorming.
statements.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1, Introduction, data provenance; markdown line 23.

statements.quote: While the previous study focused on comparing the outcomes regarding quantity, novelty, and value of individual ideas, the study at hand focuses on the breadth of exploration and, thereby, on assessing the quality of sets of ideas.
statements.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1, Introduction, previous-study scope; markdown line 23.
PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), proceedings footer, article repository and license; markdown line 29.

statements.quote: For data collection, we developed a GPT-based brainstorming app (see Figure 1 for a screenshot and the next subsection for a more detailed description), similar to the app proposed by Di Fede et al. (2022).
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1, Procedure and participants, app description; markdown line 99.

statements.quote: We selected the problem of food waste reduction (‘How can we reduce food waste?’), which was used in previous brainstorming studies (Y. Zhu et al., 2021). Afterward, we had participants select their best ideas and answer a post-questionnaire.
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1, task and questionnaire materials; markdown line 99.

statements.quote: We communicated to the participants that only suggestions in the “list of ideas” (left side of the screen) would count toward their results (i.e., not-accepted AI ideas are excluded).
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1, definition of submitted idea lists; markdown line 103.

statements.quote: We collected the data for a different study (under review) with a focus on understanding how AI suggestions affect idea quantity and quality. To collect the data, we developed a brainstorming app containing the study details, the brainstorming question, and a timer. Participants could add, edit, and remove ideas. Participants in the human+AI condition could request AI suggestions, which were displayed next to their own ideas in a separate list (3 ideas at a time). We decided to allow copying AI suggestions into the participants’ “list of ideas” instead of only using suggestions as stimuli to make the scenario more realistic. However, the GLM might also fulfill the role of a stimuli provider.
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2, Data collection instrument; markdown line 107.
PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), Figure 2, Prompt template; markdown lines 110-124.

statements.quote: Note: curly brackets indicate placeholders; all caps placeholder labels indicate parameters fixed for this study; small caps placeholder labels indicate parameters changing based on the current canvas state; portions in italic font are only included if ideas are already present in the respective lists
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), note to Figure 2; markdown line 129.

statements.quote: To produce the AI suggestions, we used OpenAI’s GLM solution ‘gpt-3.5-turbo-0301’ at a temperature of 0.9, as recommended for creative applications (OpenAI Documentation). We defined a prompt template (see Figure 2) and dynamically populated it with the study details (i.e., brainstorming question) and the current state of the brainstorming pane, i.e., content entered by the participant (ideas) and past AI ideas.
statements.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2, model settings and prompt construction; markdown line 131.

statements.quote: All tool interactions are logged for analysis.
statements.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.2, final sentence; markdown line 137.

statements.quote: To investigate the diversity of ideas, we followed the established approach of sorting all ideas into categories (Althuizen & Reichel, 2016; Nijstad et al., 2010; Ritter & Mostert, 2018). After reviewing multiple category systems on ‘food waste’, we decided to use the system of Specht and Buck (2019). The system consists of 13 categories within five clusters. We selected this category system as it was developed on user-generated contributions (tweets), which are similar in length to the ideas in our study, based on contributions from users from a Western country (US; our participants attend a Western European university), and had an appropriate granularity, i.e., number of categories (compare, e.g., Althuizen & Reichel, 2016). We had a blind-to-condition student assistant sort the ideas into the pre-defined categories (see Table 1). All but seven ideas were categorized accordingly. We excluded all non-categorized and all deleted ideas from the analysis.
statements.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.3, Data preparation and analysis, category materials and data exclusions; markdown line 141.

statements.quote: For data analysis, we processed the log data with Python scripts. To calculate descriptive and inferential statistics (incl. assumption checks), we used JASP (JASP, 2023). For visualizations, we used Tableau.
statements.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.3, analysis code/software; markdown line 143.

statements.quote: We selected a pre-defined, published category system to increase objectivity. We reported our reasoning for selecting this category system.
statements.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 429), section 5.3, Limitations, published category system; markdown line 285.

statements.quote: On a more technical note, we only used one prompt template. While we used prompt engineering, a different prompt might have yielded different results. The results might be considered a baseline, as we neither optimized for breadth nor depth of exploration. Lastly, we only used one GLM.
statements.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 429), section 5.3, Limitations, prompt materials; markdown line 287.

notes:
Checked 2026-10-10. Read all 380 lines of the markdown conversion, including the complete references; the 10-page proceedings paper (printed pp. 421-430) contains no appendix or embedded file attachment. Checked source PDF text on pages 1, 4, 5, 9 and 10 for the quoted provenance, code, materials, acknowledgment and references, and verified the public publisher PDF is byte-identical to the local file. No explicit statement offers data or code publicly or on request; no preregistration, supplementary-file citation, or research-data repository URL is stated. The form's data_and_code.data_url and code_url are both empty. The statements field retains relevant data-provenance, analysis-code and in-paper materials descriptions; these are not release promises. Quotes are transcribed from source text, with PDF line-wrap whitespace normalized and end-of-line hyphenation joined; the Figure 2 prompt retains its source lines.

No public participant-level dataset or separate code/materials package was found. The two deposits entries are publication records checked for attachments, not two confirmed data deposits. The accessible record holds only the paper and derivatives. Printed task instructions, the prompt, illustrative ideas and aggregate results do not establish release of the participant data, so they are not classified as public_partial or code_or_materials_only. The ZORA publication record could not be inspected beyond its public DataCite metadata because of a bot check. Confidence is medium for the negative availability conclusion: it describes the sources searched, not proof that no deposit exists anywhere. OSF's specified title filter does not search authors as contributors.

No missing statistic in final.open_items can be computed from a confirmed public dataset. Participant arm means/SDs/SEs/CIs for flexibility and fluency would require the individual scores or complete categorized idea logs and arm IDs. The printed 26-per-arm analyzed count is not a per-outcome participant-flow file; randomized counts, excluded arms and exclusion timing remain unconfirmed. The conflicting human-quantity claims and the accepted-versus-logged joint-quantity analysis cannot be resolved from the publication-only files. Selected printed ideas/experience quotations cannot support arm-level text diversity or homogenization measures.

The paper explicitly reuses a previous study described as under review but does not identify that study's full citation. The candidate's possible overlap with a later Memmert paper was not assumed. DataCite https://api.datacite.org/dois/10.5167/uzh-436333 returned HTTP 200 for the related publication 'Brainstorming with a Generative Language Model: Effect of Exposure to AI Ideas on Brainstorming Performance and Cognitive Load'; its abstract describes n=75, not this paper's n=52, and contains no dataset relation. This does not establish shared participants or identify an accessible c861 data file.

Searches used only Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. No web-search engine, login, account creation, author contact, access request or bot-check bypass was used. All data/HTML/PDF responses were held in memory. Repeated identical search requests are consolidated; distinct queries and failed page-size attempts are recorded. API routes used were https://api.datacite.org/dois?query=, https://zenodo.org/api/records?q=, https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/search?q=, and https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/?filter[title]=. The searches identified no relevant OSF, Zenodo or Harvard Dataverse dataset ID requiring those repositories' file APIs. The paper and form name no Dryad, Figshare or GitHub deposit.
